title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 136 [137])
hookLine: exiles weep, and the last verse is raw rage; the Church keeps it honest, not as a command

lines: SING US ONE OF THE SONGS OF SION.
cards: There's a reggae song with these words, and later a dance-floor hit. Bright, bouncy, easy to sing along to. The words come from a psalm, and the psalm is no party.
It's exiles sitting beside foreign rivers, far from home. Their city has been burned. Their Temple is gone.
And the people who carried them off stand over them and say: go on, sing us one of the songs of Sion.

teach.h: THE CITY BURNED, THE PEOPLE TAKEN.
teach.b: First, the history. The Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and carried many of its people away to Babylon. This psalm is their voice.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." They hang their instruments on the willows.
Then the taunt comes, and their answer: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Second, the vow.

teach.h: IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.
teach.b: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, the psalmist says, let my right hand be forgotten.
Jews have kept that vow close; one explanation given for the glass broken at a Jewish wedding is to remember Jerusalem even in the middle of joy. Third, the ending, and it's hard to hear.
The last verse blesses whoever would take Babylon's little ones and dash them against the rock. There's no softening it. It's the voice of people who watched their own city fall.
So what does the Church do with it? It doesn't pretend the verse isn't there.
It keeps it in the Bible as an honest cry, not a command.

teach.h: HOW SHALL WE SING THE SONG OF THE LORD?
teach.b: The psalmist doesn't act on it; he says it to God. In the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church leaves those last verses out of common prayer.
And some of the old monks read them another way: Saint Benedict, in his Rule, speaks of dashing evil thoughts against Christ, the rock, while they're still small.
That's the surprise here: the Bible lets people bring even their worst anger into prayer.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 136 [137] in the Liturgy of the Hours without its final verses, and read the whole psalm in scripture as the lament of the exiles.

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: asked for a song of Sion

s: the psalm was written as a happy song
it's the lament of exiles weeping by Babylon's rivers after their city was destroyed.
the Church cut the last verses out of the Bible

the psalmist hands his rage to God rather than acting on it

games.q: you're an exile by the river. the soldiers who burned your city order you to sing one of your songs from home. what does the psalm say?
o: sing loudly to show them you're not broken.
how shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?
games.why: they hang their instruments on the willows: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?"

practice: Notice one thing you're angry about, something done to you, or to someone you love, or something in the news, and name it plainly in your head without dressing it up.
If you pray, hand it to God as it is, rough and unfinished, the way the psalmist did. If you don't, let yourself feel it without acting on it, and breathe out slowly.

wordCard.voice: Sion. The Douay's name for Jerusalem, remembered by exiles weeping by the rivers of Babylon, in a psalm whose last verse is rage handed over to God. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: upon the rivers of Babylon, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: Your line: even anger can be prayed. The week ran from a lamp to the feet, up the pilgrim road, into Jerusalem's gates, out of the depths, to a quiet lap, and now to the rivers of exile. See you tomorrow.
